ai.definition: Quantum Encryption, specifically Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), is a method of securing communication by using the principles of quantum mechanics to ensure that any attempt at eavesdropping will be detected.
ai.howItWorks: Entangled particles are generated and used to create encryption keys. When these particles are measured, their state changes, which can be used to generate a shared secret key between communicating parties. Any third-party attempting to intercept this communication would cause disturbances that can be detected by the communicating parties, indicating potential eavesdropping.
ai.problemSolved: It addresses the issue of secure key exchange in classical cryptography where keys might be intercepted without detection, leading to compromised security.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing quantum encryption devices involves complex processes such as creating and manipulating entangled photons or ions. This often requires ultra-high vacuum environments and precise control over temperatures and electromagnetic fields.
ai.buildProcess: The process includes generating entangled particles, encoding information into these particles using optical systems, and then transmitting them through secure channels to the receiver where they are decoded back into usable keys.
ai.costDrivers: High costs stem from the need for specialized equipment like lasers, detectors, and vacuum chambers. Additionally, there is a limited supply of certain materials used in quantum devices, which can drive up prices.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook suggests continued growth as more applications are developed and integrated into existing communication networks.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks for quantum encryption are still evolving. Standards and guidelines are being established to ensure interoperability and security.
ai.risks: Technological risks include the complexity of maintaining these systems over long distances due to signal degradation. There is also a risk that current quantum devices may be vulnerable to attacks through side channels or other means.
ai.profitability: Profitability varies but shows potential in sectors requiring high levels of security, such as government communications and financial transactions.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments could include advancements in miniaturization, integration with classical cryptographic systems, and improvements in long-distance transmission technologies.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking. Long-term operation requires continuous power but can be optimized for efficiency.

glossary.def: A physical phenomenon where quantum particles become interconnected such that the state of one particle cannot be described independently of the others, even when separated by large distances.
A method for securely distributing encryption keys using principles from quantum mechanics to ensure security against eavesdropping.

subsystems.name: Photon source
subsystems.role: emits the faint light pulses or entangled pairs that carry the key.

subsystems.name: Quantum channel
subsystems.role: carries single photons from sender to receiver.

subsystems.name: Detector module
subsystems.role: counts individual photons at the far end.
parts: single-photon avalanche diodes or superconducting nanowire detectors

subsystems.name: Classical channel
subsystems.role: a normal authenticated link for protocol messages — never for the key itself.

subsystems.name: Post-processing and key management
subsystems.role: turns noisy raw detections into a short, provably secret key and stores it.

subsystems.name: Range extension
subsystems.role: bridges links beyond the reach of a single fibre span.

buildSteps.title: Secure the physical path
buildSteps.detail: Lay or lease dedicated dark fibre with low loss and stable temperature, or build a line-of-sight ground station for a satellite pass.

buildSteps.title: Build the transmitter
buildSteps.detail: A laser is attenuated to roughly one photon per pulse, then encoded in polarisation or phase; decoy pulses of varying intensity are interleaved to defeat photon-number-splitting attacks.

buildSteps.title: Build the receiver
buildSteps.detail: Detectors are cooled and aligned to the incoming photons, with random basis choice applied per pulse.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate the link
buildSteps.detail: Characterise loss and measure the quantum bit error rate; if it is too high, no key can be distilled.

buildSteps.title: Run the protocol
buildSteps.detail: Sender and receiver exchange quantum states, then compare which measurement bases they used over the classical channel. Only pulses where the bases matched are kept.

buildSteps.title: Authenticate and correct
buildSteps.detail: The classical messages are authenticated so an eavesdropper cannot impersonate either side; error correction removes mismatches from detector noise.

buildSteps.title: Amplify privacy
buildSteps.detail: Hashing compresses the corrected string, shrinking any information an eavesdropper might hold to a negligible amount and yielding the final key.

buildSteps.title: Deliver keys to the encryptor
buildSteps.detail: The key feeds a one-time pad or refreshes AES keys continuously, so traffic is re-keyed far faster than any attacker can respond.

buildSteps.title: Extend the network
buildSteps.detail: Untrusted-range links are chained through trusted nodes, or satellites distribute keys between distant ground stations; quantum repeaters remain a research goal.

prerequisites.why: keys only form if false clicks are rare; detector dark counts set the practical distance limit.

prerequisites.tech: Low-loss dark fibre or clear optical line of sight
prerequisites.why: fibre loss and free-space turbulence directly throttle the key rate and range.
without it, the classical channel can be spoofed and the quantum channel becomes pointless.
without them, key distribution over hundreds of kilometres needs trusted relays, which are not end-to-end secure.
interoperability across vendors and countries is still being defined, limiting network scale.

pathway.milestone: metro and intercity fibre QKD links running alongside conventional encryption
pathway.unlocks: key distribution whose interception is detectable in principle, used by banks, utilities and government networks.

pathway.milestone: satellite QKD between ground stations, following the Micius demonstrations from 2016 onward
pathway.unlocks: intercontinental key exchange without trusting every intermediate node.

pathway.milestone: chip-scale, mass-produced QKD modules integrated with data-centre encryptors
pathway.unlocks: drop in cost, so quantum keys become routine rather than bespoke.

pathway.milestone: quantum repeaters and memory nodes forming an entanglement-based network
pathway.unlocks: device-independent security and a path to distributed quantum computing — while post-quantum cryptography covers most ordinary needs far more cheaply.
